analysis.one_liner: Lets the government break drug monopolies and cap prices on federally funded COVID-19 treatments.
analysis.headline: The MMAPPP Act, which would have let the government override monopolies on federally funded COVID-19 drugs, was referred to committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill required that any COVID-19 drug developed with federal money be sold at a fair price and be licensable to other manufacturers on open, nonexclusive terms, so generics could compete. If the Health Department judged a pandemic drug's price excessive, the bill let it void the drugmaker's FDA exclusivity and license others to make the drug, with the original company paid a reasonable royalty. It also required drugmakers to disclose publicly how much federal money went into each COVID-19 drug. It was referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who would need COVID-19 treatments and vaccines, especially those facing racial and socioeconomic disparities in access, plus government health programs and insurers that pay for the drugs. Generic manufacturers would gain a right to produce licensed versions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: COVID-19 patients and generic drug makers

how_it_helps.text: Requires federally supported COVID-19 drug contracts to include fair-pricing terms that account for access, racial and socioeconomic disparities, and the value of federal investment [S2][S3].

Requires any federal license to a COVID-19 drug patent to be open and nonexclusive, and lets the government grant the license itself if the contractor refuses, with the company paid a reasonable royalty [S2][S3].
If HHS finds a pandemic drug's price excessive, it must void FDA-granted exclusivity and grant open licenses to other manufacturers, subject to reasonable royalties [S2][S3].

Requires COVID-19 drugmakers to report publicly, in plain language, how much of the drug's development was federally funded, along with costs, pricing, and federal benefits, with daily fines for noncompliance [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical companies developing COVID-19 drugs with federal support, which could lose monopoly pricing power and FDA exclusivity when the government deemed their prices excessive, though they would be paid reasonable royalties on licensed generic sales.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmaceutical companies with federally funded COVID-19 drugs

drawbacks.text: The bill defines 'excessive price' using flexible, multi-factor judgments by HHS rather than a clear numerical cap, which could invite political manipulation of the standard or legal challenges from drugmakers [S3].

Allowing the government to void exclusivity and license competitors could reduce companies' incentive to invest in developing new pandemic treatments, a trade-off supporters acknowledged by limiting the bill to public-health emergencies and guaranteeing royalties [S3].
Applying to drugs developed 'in whole or in part' with federal support could sweep in many drugs, raising dispute over how much government involvement should trigger the licensing requirement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the benefit was potentially large — access to affordable COVID-19 treatments and vaccines developed with taxpayer money — while the cost fell mainly on drugmakers' monopoly profits, with royalties preserving some return. The main honest concern is that government price-setting and compulsory licensing could dampen future investment in pandemic drugs, which the bill partly addressed by limiting itself to public-health emergencies and guaranteeing reasonable royalties.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health Committee, which never took it up, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tina Smith introduced the bill on August 5, 2020, with five Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, its only action [S5].
No committee markup, floor vote, or further action followed before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical companies that were developing or would develop COVID-19 drugs with federal support kept their patent and exclusivity protections and pricing power, since the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmaceutical companies kept their monopoly pricing power

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was entirely Democratic (a Democratic sponsor and six Democratic cosponsors), and the bill never advanced past committee referral [S4].

industries.note: Companies developing COVID-19 drugs with federal money would have lost the right to sole pricing power and could have had FDA exclusivity voided if prices were judged excessive, though they would have received reasonable royalties on generic production. For the public this meant potentially cheaper access to pandemic treatments [S2][S3].
Generic makers would have gained the right to produce licensed versions of federally supported COVID-19 drugs, expanding their production opportunities while lowering prices for patients [S2][S3].
